activities.caption: drag the divider — how two system families bend separation
activities.name: crFusionCompare

config.prompt: Drag the divider — two ways real systems bend the design:

before.label: parliamentary fusion
before.text: UK, Germany, Japan: the prime minister sits in Parliament and commands its majority — the separation concentrates in an independent judiciary and fixed terms.

after.label: presidential separation
after.text: All three branches kept formally separate — at the cost of 'divided government' standoffs.

config.why: Neither design is superior on paper; both depend in practice on actors staying inside their lanes — where they do out of habit, constitutions need few locks.

activities.anchor: The boldest institutional invention in this tradition
activities.caption: true or false — judicial review's claims
activities.name: crReviewJudge

statements.s: Judicial review was granted explicitly in the US Constitution's Article III.
statements.why: Chief Justice Marshall simply claimed it in Marbury v. Madison (1803) — inferred from the document's logic, not its text.

statements.s: Strong review lets courts strike down legislation.
statements.why: US, Germany, Canada, South Africa — the German court is built as a 'militant democracy' that can ban parties hostile to the constitutional order.

statements.s: The power exists in some form on every continent.
statements.why: Two centuries after Marbury, variants are everywhere.

statements.s: Marshall's reasoning: a law contrary to the constitution 'is void', and it is the judiciary's province 'to say what the law is'.
statements.why: The two phrases carry the whole claim.

activities.caption: rebuild the proportionality test, question by question
activities.name: crProportionOrder

config.prompt: The proportionality test, in the order courts ask it — assemble the sequence:
items: Is the limitation prescribed by law?
Is it pursuing a legitimate aim?
Is it the least restrictive means available?
config.why: What this makes of rights language: not absolute trump cards, but strong presumptions the state must justify overriding — a speech ban for a compelling, narrow reason survives; a blanket one does not.

activities.anchor: that is the point of the architecture
activities.caption: fill the blanks — to whom rights are promised
activities.name: crLosersCloze

config.text: Rights are promises made %%0%% the losers of elections — because a different majority will govern %%1%% and it will inherit the %%2%% limits. Majorities are not always right; that is the point.
config.hint: One preposition, one time word, one adjective for which limits get inherited.

config.prompt: How many states' cases can the European Court of Human Rights hear — against their own governments?
config.why: Cases from 46 states against their own governments — the regional court where the international floor has real teeth, though enforcement still binds reputations more reliably than armies.

activities.caption: one line of this rights briefing is wrong
activities.name: crAbsoluteSpot

config.prompt: One line of this student's rights briefing is wrong — click it:
lines: Classic rights are 'thou shalt not' constraints on the state; newer social rights are obligations to provide.
Rights collide: speech against defamation and incitement, protest against public order, privacy against press freedom.
Courts resolve collisions with a proportionality test — prescribed by law, legitimate aim, necessary, least restrictive means.
Rights operate as absolute trump cards no state may ever override.
Korematsu (upheld 1944, formally repudiated in 2018) remains the standard warning of what fear does to paper guarantees.
config.correction: Rights are strong presumptions the state must justify overriding — a speech ban for a compelling, narrow reason survives; a blanket one does not.
config.why: The real contest is never 'rights or no rights' but who decides the limits, under what test, and how easily the limit expands in a panic.
